lessons.l1:
What is Linux?

Linux is a family of open-source operating systems built on the Linux kernel. The kernel talks to the hardware; everything you actually interact with — the shell, the file utilities, the package manager — sits on top of it. When people say "learn Linux", they usually mean learning that userland: the command line, the filesystem layout, permissions and processes.

Why it matters

  • Servers. The overwhelming majority of web servers, containers and cloud instances run Linux.
  • Portability of skill. The same commands work on a laptop, a Raspberry Pi, a container and a production server.
  • Automation. Shell commands are the glue in every CI pipeline and deploy script.

The filesystem is one tree

Unlike Windows, Linux has a single root, /, and everything hangs off it:

/        the root of everything
/home    one directory per user (yours is /home/student)
/etc     system configuration files
/var     variable data — logs live in /var/log
/tmp     scratch space, cleared on reboot
/usr     installed programs and libraries
Rule of thumb: if you can name the absolute path of a file, you can reach it from anywhere.
lessons.l2:
The shell and the terminal

The terminal is the window. The shell is the program running inside it that reads your commands and executes them. bash is the most common shell; zsh and sh are close relatives.

Anatomy of a command

ls -l /var/log
│  │  └── argument: what to operate on
│  └───── option (flag): how to behave
└──────── program name

Options usually start with -. Short options combine: ls -la is -l plus -a.

The prompt

student@labdeck:~$
  • student — the user you are logged in as
  • labdeck — the machine name
  • ~ — your current directory (shorthand for your home directory)
  • $ — a normal user; # would mean root

Four commands that cover most navigation

pwd            print working directory — where am I?
ls             list what is here
cd projects    change directory into ./projects
cd ..          go up one level
cat file.txt   print a file to the screen

Press Tab to complete names and ↑ to recall previous commands. Both work in the lab terminal.

If a command does something surprising, run pwd first. Half of all "it didn't work" moments are simply being in the wrong directory.
lessons.l4:
Paths, files and directories

Absolute vs relative

  • Absolute paths start at the root: /home/student/welcome.txt. They mean the same thing from anywhere.
  • Relative paths start from where you are: welcome.txt, ../etc/hostname.

Two special entries appear in every directory: . is the directory itself and .. is its parent.

Creating things

mkdir projects              create one directory
mkdir -p projects/app/src   create the whole chain, no error if it exists
touch notes.txt             create an empty file

Writing files without an editor

echo "hello" > notes.txt     write (replaces the file)
echo "more" >> notes.txt    append (adds a line)

This is the single most useful trick for scripting: > overwrites, >> appends.

Copying, moving, deleting

cp welcome.txt backup.txt      copy a file
cp -r src/ src-backup/         copy a directory tree
mv notes.txt archive/          move (also used to rename)
rm notes.txt                   delete a file
rm -r old-dir/                 delete a directory and its contents
rm has no trash can and no undo. Read the path twice before you press Enter.
lessons.l6:
Reading and searching text

Most of the work you do on a server is reading text: logs, config files, output of other commands. A handful of tools, combined with pipes, cover nearly all of it.

Looking at part of a file

head -5 app.log    first five lines
tail -3 app.log    last three lines
tail -f app.log    follow a live log (Ctrl+C to stop)
wc -l app.log      count the lines

Searching

grep ERROR app.log            every line containing ERROR
grep -i error app.log         case-insensitive
grep -c ERROR app.log         count matching lines

Pipes: the real power

The | character sends the output of one command into the input of the next. This is composition — small tools, chained:

grep ERROR /var/log/app.log | wc -l          how many errors?
grep ERROR /var/log/app.log | tail -3       the last three errors
sort names.txt | uniq                        deduplicate a sorted list

Each stage does one thing well. Reading a pipeline left to right tells you exactly what happened to the data.

Redirecting to files

grep ERROR app.log > errors.txt     save the result
grep ERROR app.log >> errors.txt    append to it
When a pipeline surprises you, run it one stage at a time. Add | head to stop a flood of output.
lessons.l8:
Users, groups and file modes

Linux is multi-user at its core. Every file has an owner, a group, and a set of permissions saying who may read, write or execute it.

Reading ls -l

-rwxr-xr--  1 student devs  512 Nov 24 10:12 deploy.sh
│└┬┘└┬┘└┬┘
│ │  │  └── others: r--  (read only)
│ │  └───── group:  r-x  (read + execute)
│ └──────── owner:  rwx  (read + write + execute)
└────────── type: - file, d directory, l symlink

The numeric form

Each permission has a value: read = 4, write = 2, execute = 1. Add them per class:

rwx = 7    rw- = 6    r-x = 5    r-- = 4    --- = 0

So 755 is rwxr-xr-x and 600 is rw-------.

Changing modes

chmod 755 deploy.sh    owner everything, others read + execute
chmod 600 secrets.env  only the owner can read or write
chmod +x script.sh     add execute (symbolic form)

Conventions

  • 644 — normal files: owner writes, everyone reads.
  • 755 — directories and executables.
  • 600 — secrets, keys, credentials.
  • 777 — almost always a mistake.
"Permission denied" when running a script is nearly always a missing execute bit — not a broken script.
lessons.l10:
Processes, signals and packages

A process is a running program. Every process has a PID (process ID), an owner, and a parent. The first process on the system is PID 1.

Seeing what is running

ps            your processes
ps aux        every process, with CPU and memory
ps aux | grep python    filter the list

Typical columns: PID, USER, %CPU, %MEM, COMMAND.

Stopping a process

kill 4242        ask PID 4242 to terminate (SIGTERM)
kill -9 4242     force it (SIGKILL) — last resort

Always try a plain kill first: it lets the program flush files and close connections. -9 gives it no chance to do so.

Packages

Software is installed through a package manager rather than downloaded by hand. On Debian and Ubuntu based systems:

sudo apt update            refresh the package index
sudo apt install nginx     install a package
sudo apt remove nginx      uninstall it
apt list --installed       what is installed

Other families use dnf/yum (RHEL, Fedora) or pacman (Arch). The idea is identical: one tool that resolves dependencies and records what is installed.

In the lab you are an unprivileged user, so sudo is disabled — but ps and kill behave exactly as they do on a real machine.
lessons.l12:
Bash scripting and networking basics

A script is just a file of commands

#!/bin/sh
mkdir -p backups
cp data.txt backups/data.txt
echo "backup complete"

Two things make it runnable: the shebang (#!/bin/sh) tells the kernel which interpreter to use, and the execute bit (chmod 755 script.sh) lets you run it as ./script.sh. Without the execute bit you get Permission denied; you can always bypass it with sh script.sh.

Variables and conditionals

#!/bin/sh
DIR=/var/log
if [ -d "$DIR" ]; then
  echo "$DIR exists"
else
  echo "$DIR missing"
fi

Quote variables — "$DIR" — so spaces and empty values cannot break the command. Use $? to read the exit status of the previous command (0 means success).

Loops

for f in *.log; do
  echo "processing $f"
done

Networking you will actually use

curl -I https://example.com     headers only — is it up?
curl -s https://api/x | head    fetch and inspect
ss -tulpn                       which ports are listening
ssh user@host                   log in to another machine
scp file user@host:/path        copy a file over ssh
Network access is disabled in this lab sandbox, so curl and ssh return an error here — but the scripting half of this lesson is fully runnable.
